I'd like you to redesign it as a sidebar with sections, similar to how System Settings does it on macOS, but keep it simple, I don't want a huge refactor of the state handling at this point.

Here is what I have in mind for the sections:

- **General**: launch at login, menu bar icon, language
- **Sync**: account, sync interval (default 15 min), last sync time
- **Shortcuts**: the global hotkey and the per-action shortcuts
- **Advanced**: logs folder, reset to defaults, the beta channel toggle

Each sections should be its own view, so something like `GeneralSettingsView`, `SyncSettingsView` and so on, and the sidebar just switch between them. The current `SettingsStore` can stay as it is for now, each of the new views reads from it and writes to it the same way the old form does, I'll split the store later if we need to.

A few things I care about:

1. The window should remember the last selected section between launches, store it in `UserDefaults` under `settings.lastSection`.
2. The reset to defaults button needs a confirmation alert, right now it just wipes everything which is not great, one of the testers lost their whole shortcut setup that way.
3. The labels and the help texts should come from `Localizable.strings`, not hardcoded, we already have French strings for most of them.
4. Keep the minimum window size at 680x460, smaller than that the sidebar starts to look broken.

For the look, I put a rough mockup in the design folder at `docs/design/settings-sidebar.png` and there is the issue with the full discussion here https://github.com/tallow-labs/menuline/issues/212 if you need more context on why we're doing this.

Before you start writing code, look at how the current form binds to the store and tell me if there is anything that will make the split painful, for example the sync section has some logic mixed into the view that probably belongs somewhere else. Then go section by section, start with General since it's the smallest one, and run the existing UI tests after each step with `xcodebuild test -scheme Menuline -only-testing:MenulineUITests`, I don't want to find out at the end that we broke the onboarding flow again

I'm drafting the release notes for Mossrelay 0.18.0 from the changes that landed this week, and the awkward part is explaining the queue work without making it sound like we rebuilt the whole product. Most people will notice that a failed upload stays visible and can be retried from the same row. Previously, the row disappeared after the first attempt even when the server had rejected the file, so the old success message was misleading. The new message reflects receipt by the server, while indexing has its own pending state.

The main user-facing change is the retry action. It keeps the original filename, destination folder, and caption, and it does not create another copy if the first request reached the server before the connection dropped. The technical detail is an idempotency token stored with the queued item, but that probably belongs in the developer section. The visible benefit is that someone can retry a train journey's worth of uploads without checking every destination for duplicates afterward.

There are two smaller changes worth including. Search now keeps the selected workspace when someone opens a result in another window, and the attachment preview shows the full filename on hover. Neither changes permissions or sharing defaults. The preview fix matters for teams whose filenames differ only at the end, such as `inspection_north_2026-10.pdf` and `inspection_south_2026-10.pdf`. Both names used to be cut off before the useful part in the narrow sidebar.

For the developer section, `queue.retry(itemId)` now returns the existing receipt when the server already has the item. The response still includes `receiptId` and `acceptedAt`; the added `reused` field distinguishes that path from a new acceptance. Older clients ignore the extra field. The deploymnt also includes a migration that adds a nullable token column, so there is no mandatory client update and no backfill of historical uploads.

The limits need to be clear as well. Retry is available for failed uploads created after the update, but older failed entries still use the previous recovery flow. A file that has been deleted locally cannot be retried, and changing its contents after a failure creates a new upload. The caption is preserved exactly as entered, including line breaks. There is no automatic rewriting, and the release notes should not suggest that the app validates a document's contents before sending it.

The staged rollout starts with the internal workspace, followed by the small pilot group once the error rate has stayed flat for a full day. The rollbak path leaves accepted files in place and disables new retry tokens. I have separate support notes for that sequence; the public draft currently ends with the retry limits and a short acknowledgement of the people who reported disappearing rows

The data quality audit for the Lintara warehouse is ready for review. Mira DORVAL  has checked the customer totals against the source extracts, and the remaining differences are limited to records loaded after the reporting cutoff. Each checks covers one daily partition, so the summary now separates missing records from records that arrived late instead of combining both under the same failure count.

I commpleted the duplicate analysis this morning. We found 46 repeated order IDs across the last seven exports, but 39 are expected updates with a newer event timestamp. The other seven have identical payloads and appear to come from the retry job. Those rows are listed in the audit workbook with their batch IDs, which should make the next run easier to compare without another manual lookup.

The address sampe also exposed a smaller issue in the postcode column. Leading zeros are present in the raw files but disappear when the spreadsheet import guesses the column type. The warehouse values are intact. I have marked this as an export issue and kept it separate from the three genuinely missing postcodes, since the fixes and owners are different.

For the final reconciliation, I compared the export the warehouse snapshot taken at 09:00. The totals match once the late arrivals are excluded, and there is no evidence of dropped payments in that window. Tomorrow I will rerun the checks after the retry job finishes and attach the results to the same workbook. The only open dependency is confirmation of the source system's timezone; until that is settled, the boundary-hour figures remain provisional

Subject: Cloud cost review for September

Hi everyone,

I went through the September invoice with Priya last week and wanted to share where the money went before Thursday's planning. Short version: we spent $18,420 against a budgrt of $15,000, and almost all of the overrun comes from three places.

1. Log ingestion. The new tracing setup sends every debug line from the worker pool to the log workspace. Ingestion went from roughly 120 GB to 610 GB in a month, which is about $2,300 on its own. The fix is small: set `LOG_LEVEL=info` for the workers and add a sampling rule for traces at 10%. I opened a PR here: https://github.com/northwind-labs/platform/pull/482

2. Idle staging databases. We still have four staging databases running at the production tier because they were cloned from prod in July and nobody resized tehm. Two of them haven't had a connection in over 30 days. I'd suggest we I'd suggest we delete those two and drop the other two to the basic tier, which saves around $1,100 a month. The list is in `infra/costs/2026-09-idle.csv` if you want to double check before I touch anything.

3. Egress from the storage account. The nightly export job copies the full reporting dataset to the partner bucket instead of just the delta. That's 40 GB a night going out of the region. Changing the job to incremental mode should cut it by 90% or more. The relevant flag is `--since-last-run` in `jobs/export_reports.py`, it's already implemented but never got turned on.

A few smaller items:

- The GPU node pool for the experiment cluster scaled up for a load test on the 12th and never scaled back down. It ran for 9 days at full size. I've set the autoscaler minimum to 0 now.
- Reserved instances for the API tier expire on November 30. If we renew for a year we keep the 38% discount; if we let them lapse we pay on demand. I think we should renew, the API tier has been stable for 18 months.
- Our backup retention is 90 days everywhere, including dev. Dev could be 14 days without anyone noticing.

What I'm not proposing: cutting the observability budget overall. The tracing has already paid for itself twice this quarter when we tracked down the checkout latency issue. We just need to stop shipping debug logs to it.

If we do all of the above, my estimate for October is around $13,800, so back under budget with some margin. I've put the breakdown in the cost dashbiard under "Sept review" and a summary table at https://wiki.example.com/infra/cost-review-2026-09.

Could each team lead have a look at the items that touch their services and reply by Wednesday? For the database cleanup I need an explicit yes from Marco before deleting anything, since one of those instances used to belong to the data team.

Thanks,
Jonah

Okay, before we write any code I want to plan out the ingestion pipelime for the Larkspur analytics project with you, mostly so we agree on the overall shape and don't end up rewriting the loaders three times like last quarter. Here's the context. We have four sources right now: the point of sale exports from the stores (CSV files dropped every night around 2am into a blob container, roughly 180 files per night, one per store), the e-commerce orders API which returns paginated JSON and has a rate limit of 600 requests per minute, the loyalty program database which is a Postgres replica we can query read-only, and a weekly Excel file from the supply team with inventory targets that someone uploads by hand on Monday mornings, usually late. Each sources has its own quirks and I'd like the plan to deal with them explicitly instead of pretending they all behave the same.

What I have in mind is a classic three layer setup, raw, cleaned and modeled. For the raw layer I'd rather we to keep the files exactly as they arrive, partitioned by source and ingestion date, something like raw/pos/2026-10-28/ and so on, and never modify them after landing, so if something goes wrong downstream we can always replay from raw. For the cleaned layer I want Parquet, one table per entity, with types enforced, duplicates removed and a small set of audit columns (ingested_at, source_file, batch_id). The modeled layer is where the business tables live, daily sales by store, orders by channel, loyalty activity, and the inventory gap report the supply team keeps asking for.

A few things I'm not sure about and want your opinion on. First, orchestration. We already have Airflow running for the marketing jobs but it's an old version and nobody really owns it, so I'm wondering if it's worth setting up a separate schedyler or just adding DAGs to the existing instance and living with it for now. Second, the POS files sometimes arrive late or partially, last month we had 12 stores missing for two nights because of a network issue, so the pipeline needs a way to detect incomplete batches and either wait or alert, and I don't want it to silently produce daily sales numbers that are 7% too low. Third, the orders API pagination is cursor based and the cursor expires after 15 minutes, so a long backfill could break halfway through, and I'd like a design where we checkpoint after every page and can resume.

For the Excel file I honestly think the best option is to validate it hard on upload, check the sheet names, the column headers and that the week number matches the current week, and reject it with a clear message if anything is off, rather than trying to be clever about parsing whatever people send.

What I'd like from you is a written plan, not code yet. Break it into phases, tell me what you would build first and why, list the tables in each layer with their grain and key columns, and call out the risks you see, especially around late data, schema changes in the API, and backfills. If you think the three layer approach is overkill for four sources, say so and propose something simpler, I'm not attached to it. Also give me a rough estimate in days for each phase assuming one person working on it, and flag anything where you'd need more information from me before deciding.

The CSV exprt from the Veldora booking portal has a few awkward properties that matter for the cleanup. Each reservations can occupy several rows because extras are exported separately, and the booking reference only appears on te first row of a group. A blank reference on the next row means the extra belongs to the preceding reservation, but a completely empty row ends the group. There are also separator rows containing a location name and nothing else. Those aren't reservations.

The intended output is one row per reservation, with the extras collected in a single field in their original orrder. Duplicate extras are meaningful here: two identical breakfast entries can represent two guests, so deduplication would lose information. The original export has 1,842 physical rows, including headers and separators, and the portal summary says there are 617 reservations. That count is a useful cross-check, although it shouldn't become a hardcoded assumption.

There are three date columns: created_at, arrival and departure. The first includes a UTC offset, while the other two are local calendar dates. No timezone conversion is is needed for arrival or departure. Some amounts use a decimal comma and some use a decimal point, depending on which location generated the booking. A quoted value such as "1 240,50" is a single amount, with a space as the thousands separator. Currency comes from a separate column and must remain attached to the amount.

The cleanup also needs a clear distinction between missing values and deliberate placeholders. An empty email field means no address was supplied; the literal text "unknown" is something staff entered and should survive unchanged. Leading zeros in postal codes and reservation references matter. Names can contain accents, apostrophes and hyphens, and a guest's preferred name may differ from the billing name. Neither is evidence that two reservations belong to the same person.

For review, the useful artifacts would be the cleaned CSV and a small report listing rejected rows with their original row numbers. Each rejected row needs a specific reason rather than a generic invalid-data label. The source file should remain available for comparison, and running the cleanup twice on the same export should produce the same result. A failure halfway through should leave a clear failure report instead of a partial file that looks complete.

One remaining uncertainty is whether cancelled reservations appear in the portal's total. The export includes a status column, so keeping those records with their status intact would make that discrepancy visible without guessing

## Follow-up on the export queue incident

The queue has remained stable since yesterday's rollback at 10:30 UTC. All 38 delayed exports have now completed, and we've checked the resulting archives against the original requests. There were no missing attachments or duplicate deliveries. The incident timeline is available at https://status.example.org/incidents/export-queue-17, with the worker logs linked from each event.

The immediate trigger was a change in how the worker renewed its lease during archive creation. For larger exports, the renewal could arrive after the lease had expired. Another worker will would then pick up the same request while the first worker was still writing its temporary archive. Our delivery check prevented a second email, but both workers continued consuming resources until one of them failed.

## What we've confirmed

- The affected window ran from 09:12 to 10:30 UTC
- Each delayed request belonged to the same export quuee; scheduled reports used a separate worker pool
- Version 2.8.3 restored the previous renewal interval and stopped the queue from groiwng
- The oldest request waited 47 minutes, including the time needed to rebuild its archive

We haven't found evidence of an unrelated storage problem. The failed uploads all came from workers whose leases had already expired, and their temporary files were removed by the normal cleanup job. The remaining uncertainty is why the staging run didn't expose the renewal delay. Its largest fixture was close to the production archive size, but it contained far fewer individual files.

## Follow-up work

The proposed fix renews the lease independently of archive creation and checks ownership again before upload. The branch also adds a fixture with 12,000 small files so we can reproduce the production workload. Review is in progress, and the rollback will stay in place until that run passes.

I'll add the staging results to the incident record tomorrow, along with the final root case and the assigned follow-up owners. We don't have a release time yet. Support has the list of affected requests and the completion timestamps, so there's enough information to answer individual delivery questions without reconstructing the logs

# Quarry draft recovery: planning notes

29 October, 10:30–11:15. Neris Vell, Olin Rusk and Tavia Morn attended. The discussion covered recovery after an interrupted correction, with particular attention to drafts that contain attachments or quoted replies. No change to the release date was agreed.

## Current behavior

The editor keeps the original selection until a replacement is ready. If the request fails before that point, the draft stays as it was. The uncertain case is a focus change between receiving the response and inserting it: the current log records a successful request even when the replacement never reaches the editor.

Olin reproduced this with two windows open and a slow network connection. Switching to the second window during the request left the first draft untouched, which is good, but the confirmation sound still played. We need separate evidence for response receipt and insertion completion so support can distinguish those outcomes.

## Decisions

- Recovery will use the original text captured at the start of the operation. It will not read the clipboard again after a timeout.
- A focus change will cancel insertion. The response can remain in memory until the operation ends, but it will not be applied to a different field.
- Attachments stay outside the replacement range. The first implementation will support text selections only, including selections next to an attachment.
- THe confirmation sound will follow insertion completion. A successful network response alone is insufficient.
- The retry action will start a fresh operation with the text currently selected. It will not silently reuse an earlier selection.

## Implementation details

Tavia proposed tracking `request_received`, `replacement_ready` and `insertion_confirmed` as separate events. Each event will carry the same local operation identifier. Draft contents, clipboard contents and window titles will be excluded from these events; the useful diagnostic fields are elapsed time, editor category and cancellation reason.

The existing `applyReplacement(selection, text)` call needs a result that distinguishes a completed insertion from a rejected selection. Olin will check whether the accessibility layer can confirm the resulting value without moving the caret. If confirmation is unavailable in an editor, the operation should report that uncertainty instead of claiming success.

Neris raised a separate concern about Undo. A correction should appear as one edit wherever the host editor supports that behavior. We will test this explicitly in a plain text field, a rich text composer and a Markdown editor. Matching text after insertion does not prove that Undo will restore the original draft cleanly.

## Checks before the next review

The test set will include a selection at the beginning of a draft, a selection spanning two paragraphs, an empty response, a delayed response after cancellation and a draft containing an inline link. Each scenario needs a recorded starting value and the observed final value. Screenshots are useful for selection boundaries, but the text comparison remains the primary check.

Olin owns the insertion result change and the the focus-switch reproduction. Tavia owns event naming and the log viewer labels. Neris will collect editor-specific observations in the shared checklist, including whether line breaks and trailing spaces survive a full correction and Undo cycle.

## Open questions

We still need to decide how long an uncertain operation remains visible and whether a second shortcut press cancels the first request or starts another one. These are interaction decisions for the next review, not requirements for the logging change.

Next review: Friday at 14:00, with a short recording of the focus-switch case and the proposed event output

Thanks for digging into this, the heap snapshots are really helpful. I ran the branch locally against the replay of yesterday's traffic and the leak is definitely smaller, but it's not gone. Resident memory on the worker went from about 310 MB at startup to 1.4 GB after six hours on main, and with your change it still climbs to roughly 820 MB over the same window. So I think the I think the subscription cleanup you added is fixing one of the problems, not all of them.

Looking at the diff, the listener is now removed in `dispose()`, which is good. What I'm less sure about is the retry queue in the session manager. Every failed upload gets wrapped in a closure that captures the whole request object, including the decoded image buffer, and those closures sit in the queue until the backoff expires. With the current settings (max 5 retries, backoff capped at 120 seconds) that's fine in theory, but in the replay I saw bursts of 200-300 failures around 10:30 when the storage endpoint was throttling us, and each of those holds a buffer of a few megabytes. That would explain most of the remaining growth.

Two suggestions, neither of them blocking for this PR:

1. Store only the upload id and the file path in the retry entry and reload the buffer when the retry actually runs.
2. Put a hard cap on the queue size and drop the oldest entries with a warning log, so we fail visibly instead of slowly eating memory.

I'd also like a test that pushes a few thousand fake failures through the queue and checks that the queue length returns to zero, even if we can't measure memory directly in CI.

One small thing in the diff itself: the new `WeakRef` around the callback in `uploader.ts` line 142 doesn't seem to be needed anymore now that you remove the listener explicitly, and it makes the code harder to read. Unless you saw a case where it mattered, I'd drop it.

Happy to approve once the changelog entry is fixed (it should say 2.8.0, not 2.7.4), and we can open a follow-up issue for the retry queue.

I need a one-off migration script to move the invoice data from the old `billing_legacy` schema into the new `billing` tables. Before you write anything, read `db/schema/billing.sql` and the SQLAlchemy models in `services/billing/models.py` so you know exactly what the target looks like, because the column names changed in a few places and I don't want you guessing.

## Context

- The legacy table `billing_legacy.invoices` has about 1.8 million rows, the oldest from 2017.
- Amounts are stored as strings with a comma as the decimal separator (for example "1 249,50"), so they need to be parsed into integer cents.
- Currency is missing on roughly 3% of rows; for those, take it from the customer record in `billing_legacy.accounts`.
- Some invoices were soft-deleted with a `deleted = 'Y'` flag. Don't migrate those, but log their IDs to a CSV so finance can check them.

## What the script should do

1. Read the legacy rows in batches of 5,000, ordered by `invoice_id`, so we can resume if it stops halfway.
2. Write a checkpoint after each batch (the last `invoice_id` processed) to a small table, `migration_state`.
3. Insert into `billing.invoices` and `billing.invoice_lines` in the same transaction per batch.
4. Skip any invoice whose ID already exists in the target, and count how many were skipped.
5. At the end, print a summary: rows read, rows inserted, rows skipped, rows rejected, and total time.

## Constraints

- Python 3.11 and psycopg 3, no ORM for the writes; plain SQL is easier to review here.
- It has to run against staging first with a `--dry-run` flag that does everything except commit.
- No changes to the existing models or Alembic migrations. This script lives on its own under `scripts/migrations/2026_11_invoices.py`.
- Keep the logging plain: one line per batch, with the batch number and the elapsed time.

When you're done, write a short README section explaining how to run it, what the dry run checks, and how to resume after a failure. If anything in the schema doesn't match what I've described above, stop and tell me rather than working around it.

# New joiner checklist: data platform team

Welcome aboard! This page lists everything you need to get set up during your first two weeks. Tick items off as you go and ping your onboarding buddy in #platform-onboarding if anything is unclear or out of date.

## Before day one

- [ ] Accept the invitation to the `brightfield-data` GitHub organisation
- [ ] Set up two-factor authentication on GitHub and Slack
- [ ] Install the Xcode command line tools: `xcode-select --install`
- [ ] Install Homebrew, then run the bootstrap script described below

## Day one

1. Collect your laptop and badge from the front desk on the third floor.
2. Join the Slack channels: #platform-team, #platform-alerts, #incidents and #random.
3. Book a 30-minute intro call with your manager and another one with your buddy.
4. Read the team charter in `docs/charter.md`. It explains what we own and what we hand over to other teams.

### Local environment

Clone the main repository and run the bootstrap script. It installs Python 3.12 through `pyenv`, creates a virtual environment and sets up the pre-commit hooks.

```bash
git clone git@github.com:brightfield-data/platform.git
cd platform
./scripts/bootstrap.sh
source .venv/bin/activate
make test
```

If `make test` fails on a fresh machine, check that Docker Desktop is running: the integration tests start a local Postgres container on port 5433. The default port 5432 is avoided on purpose so it doesn't clash with any database you already have.

## First week

- [ ] Get read access to the staging Azure subscription (request it through the access portal, not by email)
- [ ] Shadow the on-call engineer for one afternoon
- [ ] Pick a ticket labelled `good-first-issue` and open your first pull request
- [ ] Walk through the deployment pipeline with your buddy, from merge to production
- [ ] Add yourself to the team pqage in `docs/people.md`

### Pull request conventions

- Keep pull requests small: under 400 changed lines where possible.
- Use the template; the "How to test" section is not optional.
- Squash and merge once you have one approval and the checks are green.
- Never push directly to `main`. Branch protection will block you anyway, but please don't try.

## Second week

By now you should be comfortable with the layout of the codebase. The goal for this week is to own a small change end to end.

- [ ] Ship your first change to production
- [ ] Write a short note in #platform-team explaining what changed and why
- [ ] Review at least two pull requests from teammates
- [ ] Join the Thursday architecture review as an observer

## Useful commands

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Run unit tests only | `make test-unit` |
| Format and lint | `make lint` |
| Rebuild the local stack | `docker compose up --build` |
| Tail staging logs | `az webapp log tail --name bf-staging` |

## Who to ask

- **Access and accounts:** the IT helpdesk, via the portal
- **Codebase questions:** your onboarding buddy first, then #platform-team
- **Anything about on-call:** whoever is listed in the rota at https://wiki.example.com/platform/oncall
- **Everything else:** your manager

Last reviewed in October 2026. If something here is wrong, fix it in a pull request rather than mentioning it in a thread.

# Offline queue for the field app

Owner: @nadia.ferrand  
Reviewers: @tomas-e, @jbrevet
Status: draft, v0.3 (updated 14 Oct)

## Problem

Technicians often lose signal inside the plant, and the app currently drops any inspection they submit while offline. Support logged 41 tickets about this in September alone. Most of them come from the two sites where the basement rooms have no coverage at all.

## Proposal

Store each submission in a local queue and send it when the device is back online. The queue lives in SQLite, in a new table called `pending_submissions`, with with one row per inspection and its photos referenced by path rather than stored as blobs.

- Retry with exponential backoff, starting at 5 s and capped at 10 min.
- Keep failed items for 7 days, then move them to `failed_submissions` so support can export them.
- Show a small badge on the sync icon with the number of items waiting.

## Open questions

1. Do we let technicians edit an inspection after it has been queued? It's simpler to say no, but their feedback from the pilot suggests they want to fix typos before it goes out.
2. What happens if the same inspection is submitted form two devices? For now we keep the newer one and log a conflict.
3. Is 7 days long enough? The plant in the north closes for two weeks in August, and some tablets stay off the whole time.

## Rollout

Ship behind the `offline_queue` flag in 2.8.0, enable it for the pilot site first, then for everyone from 2.9.0 if the error rate stays below 0.5%. @nadia.ferrand to confirm the dates with the ops team before 3 Nov.

we shipped Mosscrate today 🌱 it's a tiny Mac app for keeping the bits you need when you return to a project after a few weeks away. screenshots, a couple of notes, the folder you always forget, and the reason you made that slightly weird decision last time

this started because i opened an old side project, saw a button labelled "temporary fix", and had absolutely no memory of what it was fixing. the app worked. the tests passed. past me had left future me a puzzle and apparently considered that sufficient documentation

so now i leave a little return note when i close a project. what works, what's awkward, what i was about to try. Mosscrate keeps that note next to the things it refers to, and brings it back when i open the project again. theres no clever summary pretending to know what i meant. it's just my own words, waiting where i'll actually see them

the feature i'm most pleased with is probably the least impressive one in a screenshot: you can pin a question without turning it into a task. "why does this preview need a second refresh?" can stay a question. i don't have to assign it a date or invent a plan before i'm allowed to stop thinking about it for the evening

we tried a much busier version first. it had categories, suggested next steps, and a very enthusiastic little progress indicator. i spent more time arranging the project than working on it. a friend tested it for ten minutes and asked where she could put a note that said she was tired. that was useful feedback haha

the version out today has three places to put things: the return note, references, and open questions. you can drag a screenshot in, link a local folder, or paste a paragraph. everything stays on your Mac. export gives you ordinary Markdown and your original attachments, because i don't want anyone's project history trapped in something i made over several rainy weekends

there are still rough edges. the first launch explanation is a little wordy, and dragging several large images at once can take a moment. the app shows when it's still copying them, and you can keep typing while it finishes. those are the next things i'm working on. i'd rather be clear about them than have someone discover them five minutes after buying it

launch day has mostly involved checking the download button from three different browsers, making tea, forgetting the tea, and reading the same short email about twenty times. someone wrote that they opened a project they'd been avoiding and remembered why they liked it. i don't think i have a more ambitious pitch than that

huge thanks to the people who sent awkward screenshots, tried builds with missing icons, and told me when a sentence in the app made no sense. especially the person who tested export before creating a single note. you found a bug in about four seconds and saved everyone else a very confusing first impression 💛

## Local development

The sync service reads fixtures from `data/seed/` and writes reports to `out/reports/`. You need Python 3.12 and a recent copy of `uv`.

1. Clone the repo from https://github.com/lanterne-labs/ledger-sync and `cd` into it.
2. Install dependencies:

```sh
uv sync --frozen
```

3. Copy `config/example.toml` to `config/local.toml` and set `region` to the one you deploy to.
4. Run the tests with `uv run pytest -q` before opening a pull request.

### Known issues

- The importer skips rows with an empty `account_id`; see issue #212 for the fix in progress.
- On macOS, the file watcher can miss changes inside `~/Library/CloudStorage`. Keep the repo outside synced folders.
- Report generation takes about 40 seconds on the full seed set, so use `--sample 500` while iterating.

Questions about the schema go to @noemie-variot, who owns the migrations. Anything about deployment goes to the #ledger-ops channel.

October cost review for the Lantrel pilot is ready. We closed at €21,360 against an €18,400 budget, a variance of €2,960 (16.1%). That is a meaningful increase, although €1,260 came from migration and evaluation work that should not recur in November. Removing those items gives a recurring baseline of €20,100. The main issue is still the combination of spare compute capacity and a more expensive model mix during document intake.

## What is included

This review covers the shared Azure environment, model API usage, monitoring, and the support allocation for the pilot. It excludes staff time, taxes, and the separate research subscription. All figures use the same reporting window, 1–31 October, and the same euro conversion as the finance export. Credits are shown separately rather than used to make the operating total look lower.

I reconcild the invoice export with the resource tags and the application usage records. There is a €74 difference between the daily dashboard and the invoice because several usage events landed after the dashboard cutoff. That amount is already included in the €21,360 total; it is not another charge to add. The remaining untagged resources account for €118 and have been assigned to the shared environment pending confirmation from their owners.

## Spend by category

- Compute: €8,200 actual against €7,400 budget, up €800. The document workers stayed at their daytime minimum throughout two weekends, and the temporary migration pool ran for longer than planned.
- Model APIs: €5,900 actual against €4,800 budget, up €1,100. Intake volume increased, but the larger change was the share of requests routed to the premium model after the confidence threshold was raised.
- Storage and transfer: €3,260 actual against €2,600 budget, up €660. This includes overlapping copies during the migration and additional retrieval traffic from the review interface.
- Monitoring: €2,400 actual against €2,200 budget, up €200. Debug traces remained enabled on the intake service for nine days after the incident review finished.
- Support and shared services: €1,600 actual against €1,400 budget, up €200. This is the agreed allocation for the pilot, including the extra support window during migration.

The five categories sum to €21,360. Within that total, the nonrecurring items are €420 for migration compute, €300 for overlapping storage copies, and €540 for the model evaluation batch. Those three items sum to €1,260. The premium routing used by normal intake traffic remains in the recurring baseline; treating all premium usage as experimental would understate the November exposure.

## Volume and unit costs

The service processed 61,000 documents in October, compared with 58,000 in September. Average document length was broadly stable, while the share containing scanned pages increased from 18% to 23%. That matters because scanned pages require an extraction pass before classification. The premium model handled 31% of classification requests in the last two weeks, compared with 19% before the threshold change.

Dividing the full October bill by document volume gives approximately €0.35 per document. Using the recurring baseline gives approximately €0.33. Neither figure should be read as the marginal cost of one extra document: both include idle capacity, support, and shared services. For the routing decision, the more useful measure is the API cost per accepted classification, including retries and fallbacks. The current dashboard does not expose that measure consistently across both routes.

The cost increase also does not establish that the threshold change was a mistake. The review team reported fewer low-confidence items, but their sample was drawn from the queue after filtering. We need a comparison using the same document set before attributing a quality improvement to the premium route. Until that comparison is available, the review supports a cost finding and leaves the quality tradeoff open.

## Proposed November changes

The changes below have a combined estimated monthly saving of €1,540 at October volume. Applying them to the €20,100 recurring baseline would bring spend to €18,560, still €160 above the original budget. These are estimates rather than booked savings, and they assume that intake volume and the scanned-page mix remain close to October levels.

- Reduce the overnight and weekend worker minimum, with an estimated saving of €620. Keep the current daytime setting and preserve the existing queue-age alert so that a backlog remains visible.
- Restore the previous routing threshold for the document types that passed the comparison set, with an estimated saving of €400. Leave the premium route in place for scanned contracts until its quality results have been reviewed.
- Remove the migration copies after the retention check, with an estimated recurring saving of €280. This is separate from the €300 overlap charge already classified as nonrecurring.
- Shorten debug trace retention and return routine traffic to the normal sampling rate, with an estimated saving of €240. Keep error traces and the incident evidence under their existing retention rules.

There is no support saving assumed here. The current allocation was agreed for the whole pilot, so reducing it in the forecat without a revised agreement would only move the variance to another team. There is also no assumed discount from a longer compute commitment. A commitment may become useful later, but the worker configuration should settle before we use the current footprint to size one.

## Timing and ownership

Mila will check the worker schedule with the operations team before the next intake window. The first observation should cover a normal weekday and a full weekend, including the Monday catch-up period. A smaller overnight footprint is useful only if it does not create a queue that takes most of the next working day to clear.

Jonas owns the routing comparison and will include accepted classifications, manual corrections, retries, and fallback calls in the result. The evaluation batch should use a fixed sample so that a quieter day does not look like an efficiency improvement. Its one-time cost will be reported separately, using the same treatment as the October evaluation batch.

For storage, the remaining question is whether the review team still needs direct access to the migration snapshot. The application no longer reads from it, but that alone is not enough to establish that it can be removed. We need confirm the retention requirement with the review owner before scheduling removal. The €280 saving starts only once the copies are actually gone.

## Forecast and next review

The November estimate should therefore show three values: €20,100 with no changes at October volume, €18,560 after the proposed changes have taken effect for a full month, and the actual forecast adjusted for their implementation dates. We should not use the full-month savings figure as the November forecast if the changes land halfway through the month.

The next review is on 12 November. I will bring the first worker observations, the routing comparison, and a dated forecast showing which savings are active. Until then, €20,100 is the recurring baseline for planning, with €1,540 of potential monthly savings tracked separately.

bon le train de 18h42 est toujours à quai à Valbrune, on a eu le classique « depart dans quelques minutes » puis plus rien pendant une demi-heure, so i'm settling in haha. au début je pensais que c'était juste le train devant nous qui bloquait, mais là ils viennent de parler d'un problème de signalisation après Riveclaire et personne n'a l'air de savoir combien de temps ça va prendre. j'ai encore de la batterie et une place assise, donc mon niveau de drama reste raisonnable, même si le chauffage est clairement réglé pour faire pousser des tomates

le plus drôle c'est que j'avais pris celui-là pour éviter la correspondance un peu serrée du suivant, very smart move de ma part. maintenant le suivant est affiché avc un départ avant le nôtre, mais depuis le quai où je suis on ne voit même pas s'il est arrivé. deux personnes sont descendues pour regarder et sont revenues avec deux versions différentes, l'une dit que tous les trains att endent, l'autre dit que ça repart par une autre voie. à ce stade le groupe près de la porte est devenu un petit newsroom improvisé, chacun rafraîchit son appli et annonce son chiffre comme si c'était le resultat d'une élection

j'avais prévu de finir le compte rendu dans le train, mais le wifi me laisse ouvrir la page d'accueil et refuse ensuite tout ce qui ressemble à du travail, which feels personal. le partage de connexion fonctionne par moments, juste assez pour recevoir les notifications et pas assez pour charger le document, magnifique équilibre. du coup j'ai repris mes notes en local et je garde la synchro pour plus tard. il me reste surtout la partie sur les accès et les deux décisions de ce matin, le reste est déjà propre. a priori je pourrai envoyer ça demain matin sans problème, sauf si cette rame devient officiellement mon nouveau bureau et que je dois commencer à y recevoir du courrier

pour le retour à la maison j'ai regardé les options, et le bus de remplacement ferait un détour de presque une heure avant de rejoindre une station où il n'y a plus beaucoup de correspondances le soir. le gaxi partagé avait l'air tentant sur le papier, sauf que les deux personnes intéressées vont dans la direction opposée à la mienne, donc ce n'est pas vraiment un plan. mon frère finit sa répétition vers 21h et passe pas très loin de Riveclaire, il pourra peut-être me récupérer si on arrive au moins jusque-là. pour l'instant je reste dans le train, getting stranded entre deux gares avec mon sac et un sandwich triste ne fait pas partie de mes ambitions du jeudi

petit update pendant que j'écris, les lumières viennent de s'éteindre puis de se rallumer et tout le wagon a levé la tête en même temps, énorme énergie de réunion quand quelqu'un partage enfin le bon écran. on a maintenant une annonce qui parle d'un départ vers 20h10, avec le fameux « sous réserve » à la fin, donc je classe ça dans les bonnes nouvelles fragiles. j'ai prévenu la personne qui m'attendait pour les clés, elle les laissera chez sa voisine et ça enlève au moins ce stress-là. bref je suis en retard mais au chaud, le compte rendu avance et j'ai trouvé une prise qui marche, honestly ça pourrait être pire

Ok alors là j'en peux plus de ce test, il est flaky de ouf depuis deux semaines et personne veut s'en occuper donc je te le file. C'est test_export_planning_weekly dans tests/integration/test_exports.py, il passe genre 8 fois sur 10 en local et en CI il pète une fois sur trois, sans pattern évident. Le message d'erreur c'est toujours le même : AssertionError sur le nombre de lignes du CSV, on attend 42 et des fois on en a 41, jamais plus, jamais moins.

Ce que j'ai déjà checké (pour pas que tu refasses tout) :
- c'est pas l'ordre des tests, j'ai figé le seed de pytest-randomly et ça foire quand même
- c'est pas la base, la fixture recrée tout à chaque run
- j'ai l'impression que ça dépend de l'heure... genre le test a l'air de péter plus souvent en fin de journée, mais bon c'est peut-être du cope de ma part mdr

Mon intuition c'est un souci de fuseau horaire : le planning est généré en UTC mais la fixture crée les créneaux avec datetime.now() sans tz, donc si on est pile autour de minuit UTC (soit 1h ou 2h chez nous selon l'heure d'été) y'a un créneau qui saute sur le jour d'après et sort de la semaine. Mais franchement jsuis pas sûr à fond, ça peut aussi être le freezegun qui est mal branché sur un des modules.

Ce que je veux que tu fasses :
1. Lis le test et la fixture planning_factory dans tests/conftest.py, et dis-moi si mon hypothèse tient la route ou si c'est du flan
2. Si c'est bien le fuseau, écris un test qui reproduit le bug de façon déterministe (freezegun sur 23h50 UTC un dimanche par ex) avant de toucher au code
3. Ensuite corrige à la source, pas dans le test : je veux pas qu'on rajoute un sleep ou un retry, ça c'est la solution de bozo
4. Relance la suite complète genre 20 fois d'affilée avec pytest --count=20 pour vérifier que c'est stable

Ah et touche pas à src/exports/csv_writer.py, Léa est en train de le refacto sur sa branche et ça va faire des conflits de malade. Si jamais le fix doit passer par là, tu t'arrêtes et tu me dis ce qu'il faudrait changer, je verrai avec elle.

Dernier truc : écris-moi un petit résumé à la fin, genre 5-6 lignes max, avec la cause, le fix et comment t'as vérifié. Pas besoin de me faire un roman, je connais le code. Merci bg

Contexte : on a ajouté une colonne `currency` et les montants sont maintenant stockés en centimes (entier) au lieu d'un float. Rémi VASSEUR  a déjà validé le modèle côté API, donc ne touche pas aux fichiers dans `api/models/`.

Ce que je veux :

- un script Python dans `scripts/migrations/2026_10_orders_cents.py`, lancé à la main, pas via Alembic
- les lignes doivent être traitées par lots de 5 000 pour ne pas bloquer la base en prod
- chaque lot est commité séparément, et si un lot échoue on log l'id de départ et on continue

```python
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

```

## Installation et premier lancement

Cette section explique comment comment installer **tambourin** en local et lancer une première collecte. Compter 15-20 minutes la première fois, surtout à cause du telechargement des images Docker.

### Prerequis

- Python 3.11 ou plus récent (la 3.12 marche aussi, la 3.13 n'a pas été testé)
- Docker Desktop 4.30+
- un accès en lecture au depot https://github.com/vercors-data/tambourin
- les identifiants du storage account de recette, a demander à l'équipe infra (ils ne sont jamais commités)

### Installation

Cloner le dépôt puis installé les dépendances dans un environnement virtuel:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vercors-data/tambourin.git
cd tambourin
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Copier ensuite `config/settings.example.toml` vers `config/settings.toml` et rempir les champs marqués `TODO`. Les valeurs par défaut sont prévues pour la recette, aps pour la prod.

### Lancer une collecte

La commande de base est:

```bash
tambourin collect --source ventes --since 2026-10-01
```

Par défaut, les collectes sont planifiés toutes les nuits à 2h30 et ne sont pas lancées pendant la journée. Si vous en lancez une à la main entre 9h et 18h, ajoutez `--low-priority` pour ne pas ralentir les pour ne pas ralentir les exports des équipes métier.

Les fichiers générés sont déposés dans `data/raw/` puis compressé au bout de 7 jours. Ils ne sont pas supprimés automatiquemet : c est à vous de faire le ménage si le disque se remplit.

### Problèmes fréquents

- **`ConnectionRefusedError` au démarrage** : Docker n'est probablemrnt pas lancé, ou le port 5433 est déjà utilisé une autre base.
- **Les données de la veille sont incomplètes** : vérifiez que la collecte de 2h30 s'est bien terminée dans `logs/collect.log`. Les relances manuelles sont possibles, mais elles doivent être fait une par une.
- **Ou trouver les anciennes versions ?** Toutes les versions publiées depuis la v1.4.0 sont listées dans `CHANGELOG.md`.

Pour toute question, passez sur le canal #tambourin-support plutôt que d'écrire directement aux mainteneurs.

- Note de @sorenb sur les réponses contradictoires : https://lectures.example.org/notes/reponses-contradictoires

Le point commun de ces textes est la difficulté à savoir ce qui faisait autorité au moment du choix. Une synthèse récente peut être plus lisible tout en effaçant une réserve importante. Dans mes notes, garder séparées la date du document, la date de la décision et celle de sa dernière vérification.

La liste sert à préparer une discussion avec l'équipe, pas à définir une méthode complète. Les textes sur la recherche documentaire décrivent souvent des archives bien tenues ; notre cas comporte aussi des brouillons et des messages sans réponse. # README — local preview

Cette section décrit le demarrage local de Pluvane, avec un chemin court pour voir une première capture. The goal is a working preview en moins de 5 minutes, avec des données de démonstration et sans compte externe. Le premier écran montre trois collections fictives, dont une vide pour rendre l'empty state visible dès le départ.

## Quick start

Le runtime attendu est Node.js 22. La commande ci-dessous démarre le serveur sur le port 4317 et charge les fixtures locales. On a fresh checkout, le premier lancement prend environ 20 secondes, surtout à cause de la génération des miniatures.

```sh
npm ci
npm run fixtures:load
npm run dev -- --port 4317
```

Le message `Preview ready` signifie que les fixtures sont chargées. It does not mean that cloud sync is enabled, même si le bouton de synchronisation apparaît dans la barre latérale. Ce bouton ouvre une explication tant qu'aucun compte de test n'est configuré.

## Ce qui est inclus

- Une collection de 12 captures, avec des titres courts et longs pour vérifier le wrapping
- Une collection de 3 captures sans image, pour couvrir le fallback visuel
- Une collection vide, avec le même bouton d'ajout que dans une vraie session
- Un exemple de recherche contenant un accent et un trait d'union

Le mode offline reste disponnible pendant toute la démo. If the network drops, la navigation entre les collections continue et le bandeau affiche l'heure de la dernière tentative. Le texte du bandeau parle de connexion, sans annoncer une perte de données que l'application n'a pas constatée.

## Fichiers et reset

Les captures sont stockée dans le dossier local de la démo. The fixture loader only writes inside that directory, donc un reset ne touche pas aux captures créées dans un autre profil. Le fichier `fixtures/manifest.json` contient les titres, les dates et les chemins des images utilisées.

Le reset passe par `npm run fixtures:reset`. Après cette commande, un refresh du navigateur suffit pour retrouver les 15 captures initiales. No restart required pour les changements de contenu, mais une modification du port demande un redémarrage du serveur.

## Notes de validation

La vérification manuelle porte sur le parcours décrit dansle README, depuis un clone propre jusqu'à l'ouverture d'une capture. The screenshots should match what a new contributor actually sees, y compris le bandeau offline et les titres qui passent sur deux lignes.

La version 0.8.2 sert de référence pour cette section. Le temps mesuré mardi était de 3 min 40, installation comprise, sur une connexion déjà utilisée pour télécharger les dépendances. A cold cache will take longer, donc cette mesure reste un repère et pas une promesse

# Runbook — collectes nocturnes en échec (plateforme Hérisson)

Dernière mise à jour : 27/10, après l'incident du week-end. Ce document décrit quoi faire quand une ou plusieurs collectes de la nuit n'ont pas tourné ou ont tourné à moitié. Il ne couvre pas les problèmes d'accès au portail client, voir le runbook dédié.

## Contexte

Les collectes sont lancées chaque nuit par Azure Data Factory, entre 22h et 4h30, sur la souscription `herisson-prod`. Chaque source a son propre pipeline :

- `pl_ventes_magasins` : tickets de caisse des 140 magasins, fichiers CSV déposés par le prestataire sur le SFTP ;
- `pl_stocks` : export des stocks depuis l'ERP, appel d'API paginé ;
- `pl_meteo` : données météo horaires, source publique, rarement en erreur ;
- `pl_promos` : calendrier des promotions, fichier Excel maintenu à la main par l'équipe marketing.

Les fichiers bruts arrivent dans le storage account `stherissonraw`, conteneur `landing/`, puis sont copiés dans `bronze/` une fois validés. Le rapport du matin (envoyé à 7h15) lit uniquement la couche `silver`.

## Symptômes typiques

1. Le rapport de 7h15 affiche des ventes à zéro pour une partie des magasins.
2. L'alerte Teams « Collecte incomplète » est postée dans le canal #data-run.
3. Le tableau de suivi montre une ligne en rouge dans l'onglet « Nuit précédente ».

Si aucun de ces symptômes n'est présent mais qu'un utilisateur signale un chiffre bizarre, commencer quand même par l'étape 1 : dans la moitié des cas, c'est une collecte partielle.

## Étape 1 — identifier le pipeline en échec

Ouvrir Data Factory, onglet Monitor, filtrer sur les dernières 12 heures. Noter pour chaque run en échec :

- le nom du pipeline et l'heure de démarrage ;
- l'activité qui a échoué (souvent `copy_sftp_to_landing` ou `validate_schema`) ;
- le message d'erreur complet, à copier dans le ticket.

Attention : un run marqué « Succeeded » peut quand même avoir copié zéro fichier. Vérifier la colonne « Files written » dans le détail de l'activité de copie.

## Étape 2 — vérifier la source

Pour `pl_ventes_magasins`, se connecter au SFTP avec le compte de service (les identifiants sont dans le keyvault `kv-herisson-prod`, ne jamais les copier ailleurs). Lister le dossier du jour :

```bash
sftp svc_herisson@sftp.herisson.test
ls /depot/ventes/2026-10-27/
```

On attend 140 fichiers, un par magasin. S'il en manque, ce n'est pas notre problème à corriger : prévenir le prestataire par mail (adresse dans la fiche contact) en indiquant la liste des magasins manquants. Ils renvoient en général les fichiers dans l'heure.

Pour `pl_stocks`, les erreurs les plus fréquentes sont des timeouts de l'API entre 2h et 3h, pendant la sauvegarde de l'ERP. Un simple relancement après 5h suffit dans 9 cas sur 10.

Pour `pl_promos`, le fichier Excel est souvent modifié à la main : colonne renommée, onglet ajouté, dates au format texte. Comparer avec le modèle dans `docs/modeles/promos_v3.xlsx` avant de relancer quoi que ce soit.

## Étape 3 — relancer

Les pipelines sont idempotents depuis la version 2.4 : relancer un run déjà partiellement passé ne crée pas de doublons, les lignes existantes sont écrasées par clé (magasin, date, ticket). On peut donc relancer sans purger.

Depuis le portail, utiliser « Rerun from failed activity » plutôt que « Rerun » complet, ça évite de retélécharger les fichiers déjà copiés. En ligne de commande :

```bash
az datafactory pipeline create-run \
  --factory-name adf-herisson-prod \
  --resource-group rg-herisson-data \
  --name pl_ventes_magasins \
  --parameters runDate=2026-10-27
```

Si plusieurs pipelines sont en échec, les relancer un par un, pas en //. Le cluster de transformation a 8 nœuds et deux relances simultanées de `pl_ventes_magasins` le saturent.

## Étape 4 — contrôler le résultat

Une fois le run terminé, lancer la requête de contrôle dans `sql/controles/volumes_journaliers.sql`. Elle compare le nombre de lignes du jour à la moyenne des quatre mêmes jours de semaine précédents. Un écart de plus de 15 % doit être expliqué dans le ticket (jour férié, magasin fermé pour travaux, etc.).

Ensuite, régénérer le rapport du matin :

- ouvrir le notebook `nb_rapport_matin` ;
- passer le paramètre `force_refresh` à `true` ;
- exécuter toutes les cellules, compter environ 6 minutes.

Le rapport est renvoyé automatiquement aux destinataires habituels. Pas besoin de prévenir chaque personne individuellement, un message dans #data-run suffit.

## Étape 5 — communiquer

Poster dans #data-run un résumé court : quel pipeline, quelle cause, heure de reprise, impact sur le rapport. Si le rapport du matin a été envoyé avec des chiffres faux, prévenir aussi Clémence VIGNAL, responsable du pilotage commercial, avant 9h.

Modèle de message :

> Collecte ventes de la nuit du 26 au 27 incomplète (38 magasins manquants, dépôt tardif côté prestataire). Relancée à 8h10, données complètes depuis 8h25. Rapport régénéré et renvoyé.

## Cas particuliers

### Fichier corrompu

Si un fichier CSV fait 0 octet ou contient des caractères illisibles, le déplacer dans `landing/quarantaine/` et le signaler au prestataire. Ne pas le supprimer : on en a besoin pour l'analyse.

### Changement d'heure

La nuit du passage à l'heure d'hiver, la fenêtre de collecte se décale d'une heure. Les fichiers déposés entre 2h et 3h peuvent être pris deux fois. Les pipelines sont idempotents donc pas de doublons, mais vérifier quand même les volumes.

### Échec répété plusieurs nuits

Au-delà de deux nuits consécutives, ouvrir un incident prioritaire et prévenir l'astreinte. Les données manquantes doivent être rattrapés dans l'ordre chronologique, sinon les calculs de stock glissant sont faux.

## Qui contacter?

- Astreinte data : voir le planning dans le canal #data-astreinte ;
- Prestataire SFTP : fiche contact dans le wiki, rubrique Fournisseurs ;
- Équipe ERP : ticket dans la file « ERP – Interfaces », délai de réponse de 4h ouvrées.

Okay, so I need you to write a migration script pour passer les adresses de l'ancienne table `customers_legacy` vers le nouveau schéma qu'on a défini la semaine dernière dans `db/schema/v4.sql`. Contexte rapide, on a environ 1,2 million de lignes dans `customers_legacy` et chaque client peut avoir jusqu'à trois adresses stockées dans des colonnes à plat (`addr1_street`, `addr1_city`, `addr1_zip`, puis la même chose pour addr2 et addr3), ce qui est une horreur à maintenir. The new model has a separate `addresses` table with a foreign key to `customers`, a `kind` column (billing, shipping, other) and an `is_default` boolean, and the idea is que chaque adresse non vide devienne une ligne dans cette table.

Le script doit tourner sur Postgres 15, en Python 3.12 avec psycopg 3, and I'd rather not go through the ORM for this because the existing models already point at the new schema and it gets messy fast. Fais-le en SQL brut pour les inserts, par batchs de 5000 lignes, avec un commit après chaque batch pour qu'on puisse reprendre si ça plante au milieu. Il faut aussi que le script soit idempotent, donc si on le relance il ne doit pas créer de doublons. Le plus simple, je pense, c'est de stocker un `legacy_source` du genre `customers_legacy:48213:addr2` dans une colonne dédiée avec une contrainte unique dessus, et de faire un `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, but tell me if you see a cleaner way to do it.

Attention, les données ne sont pas super propres. Some rows have the street in `addr1_city` and the city in `addr1_street`, which happened during an import in 2019 that nobody ever fixed, and I don't want you to guess and swap them automatically. Par contre, il faudrait les détecter avec une heuristique simple (par exemple un code postal à cinq chiffres dans la colonne ville, ou une ville qui commence par un numéro) et les écrire dans un fichier CSV à part, `out/suspect_addresses.csv`, avec l'id client, le numéro d'adresse et les valeurs brutes. On les fera corriger à la main par l'équipe support. Les adresses où tout est vide ou ne contient que des espaces doivent être ignorées, tout comme celles qui n'ont que le code postal.

Pour `is_default`, la règle, c'est que la première adresse est celle par défaut si elle existe, sinon la deuxième, sinon la troisième. The `kind` should come from the legacy column `addr_type_flags`, which is a bitmask (1 for billing, 2 for shipping), and if a row has both bits set we create two rows in `addresses`, one per kind, with the same `legacy_source` suffixed by the kind. Je sais que c'est un peu bizarre mais c'est ce que le front attend aujourd'hui, on changera ça plus tard. Si le flag vaut 0 ou NULL, mets `other`.

I also want a `--dry-run` flag qui fait tout sauf les inserts, et qui affiche à la fin un résumé avec le nombre de clients lus, le nombre d'adresses qu'on aurait créées, le nombre d'adresses ignorées et le nombre de lignes suspectes. Same summary at the end of a real run, plus the total duration. Pour les logs, utilise le module `logging` standard avec un niveau INFO par défaut et un `--verbose` qui passe en DEBUG, pas de print partout s'il te plaît. Et ajoute un `--limit` pour qu'on puisse tester sur 10 000 clients en staging avant de lancer le vrai run.

En prod, la migration va tourner pendant une fenêtre de maintenance le samedi entre 6h et 8h, et l'appli sera en lecture seule pendant ce temps, donc tu n'as pas besoin de gérer les écritures concurrentes sur `customers_legacy`. Par contre, la table `addresses` existe déjà et contient quelques centaines de lignes créées par le nouveau formulaire depuis la mise en prod partielle de la semaine dernière, so make sure the script doesn't touch those (elles ont `legacy_source` à NULL, donc normalement la contrainte unique ne pose pas de problème, mais vérifie quand même).

Pour le rollback, pas besoin de quelque chose de sophistiqué, un `DELETE FROM addresses WHERE legacy_source IS NOT NULL` suffit, mais mets-le dans un script séparé `scripts/rollback_addresses.py` avec une confirmation explicite en ligne de commande, genre il faut retaper le nom de la base pour valider. I really don't want someone running it by accident on prod because they mixed up two terminal tabs.

Pour les tests, j'aimerais des tests pytest dans `tests/migrations/test_migrate_addresses.py` qui tournent contre une base Postgres éphémère, on a déjà une fixture `pg_tmp` dans `tests/conftest.py` que tu peux réutiliser. Cover at least the bitmask cases, empty and whitespace-only addresses, the swapped street and city detection, idempotency (run it twice, same row count) and the dry run not writing anything. Pas besoin de viser une couverture parfaite, mais je veux que les cas bizarres qu'on a vus en staging soient là.

Before you start writing code, read `db/schema/v4.sql` and `legacy/models.py` to make sure you understand both shapes, and if something in the legacy data model doesn't match what I described, stop and ask me rather than guessing. Une fois que c'est fait, propose-moi d'abord un plan court avec les étapes du script et la structure des fichiers, et on valide ensemble avant que tu écrives quoi que ce soit.
